Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.

- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.

- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why4: For an audience of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, a text-first (or captioned or ASL) interviewer should be its own option, not just a line in the hint, and "lock and record" is worded oddly next to the other face choices.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed, and nothing about AirCaps or my roles leaks to the people being asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions? Options: the AI interviewer on video with captions always on (Keel's pick); text only, no video, read and tap; your own recorded face. Hint: everyone can read and type or tap instead of talking.

screens.why1: Once I've said who asks the questions, it makes sense to pick how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents answer before the link goes out.
screens.why2: Daphne, read and tap, speak or type: plain words I'd understand on first read.
screens.why3: I know my people, and many would rather read than listen to a video voice, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete, but the Daphne option leads with 'asks aloud' and 'answer by talking' for an audience that may not hear or speak; it should say every question is captioned and nothing needs hearing.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and my pick of Read and tap stays as I chose it.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (read each question, tap or type; nothing needs hearing or speaking) / AI interviewer Daphne (captioned video, every question on screen; answer by typing, tapping or talking) / Let them choose

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how people answer, the natural last step is deciding who receives the link, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: Plain to me as the founder, though the second option slips from 'I' to 'you' ('Keel makes a link for each one, and you send them'), which jars slightly against the other two.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd send it to: the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already know from TranscribeGlass days, by name.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and my pick (people I know by name) is there, but there's no way to say 'a mix', and in practice I'd send named links and also post in a HLAA chapter or Deaf community group; the voice shift in option two is a small oddity too.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and my answer, each person by name, is kept as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a Keel Contacts list (Keel makes a link for each, I send them) / A group, with one open link I post where they already are / A mix of these

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is up top, but the number beside it is the median of 4 days, which sits inside my 4-to-7 range; the number that actually decides it (4 of 7 at or beyond, bar 5, 1 short) is only on the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: The Prevalence and Current solution lines read at once, but the Frequency card says the split three times over and Importance prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so those need a second look.
screens.why_b3: The four dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked: at least 8 in 10, 4 to 7 days out of 7, following what's said in the top two, today's way falls short.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what the Frequency split means for AirCaps, such as whether to target the people who have it 4+ days or whether a 2-to-3-day user still buys; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every line, but a 7-person sample against an '8 in 10 of US deaf and hard-of-hearing adults' belief is never called small, and a median of 4 under 'People disagree' could read as near-holding.
screens.instead: Frequency is split, 4 of 7 at 4+ days against a bar of 5, one person short; with only 7 answers, ask more people or narrow the wedge to those who lose the thread most days before betting the price on daily use.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven cells, all for me, on an axis from 0 to 7, with my bar marked at 6 (at least 8 in 10), so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits read at once.
screens.why_b3: "Lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people" and "at least 8 in 10" are mine, but the card says plain "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults" and drops my segment's "in the US who talk with hearing people every week".
screens.why_b4: It tells me the problem is common among these 7 and that the open questions are how often and whether it matters, which is exactly where the stage page's Frequency disagreement sends me.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 7 counted), and the small group is named as "a lean, not a call", so 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people in the last 7 days.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside the deciding numbers: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4-day low against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short, with the median of 4 days.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts days out of 7, shows my 4-to-7 band with the median at 4, and the strip shows 7 cells against a marker at 5, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Frequency and states my clause in my words: losing the thread of a conversation with hearing people on 4 to 7 days out of 7.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the split and defers with "whether it matters is the next card"; it doesn't say what the split means for me, such as narrowing to group or noisy occasions or lowering my range to 2 to 3 days.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called "a lean, not a call", but the Asked line's tag "the most recent time it happened" misdescribes a count over 7 days and makes me wonder whether only one occasion was read.
screens.instead: Drop "the most recent time it happened" from the Asked line, and have the So line say: "Nearly half lose the thread on fewer than 4 days; consider whether your wedge is people with daily group or noisy conversations, or whether 2 to 3 days is the truer low."

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against the bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: I can see what is counted and where the bar is, but the caption says each of the 7 picked two while the bars add to 13, so one person must have stopped at one; I had to add the bars up to see that.
screens.why_b3: Importance and my own row, Following what hearing people are saying, are my words, set against my four rivals as five things, and the occasion is my conversation with hearing people.
screens.why_b4: The So line carefully says top two, not first, but it doesn't tell me what that means for AirCaps; for example, that 3 of 7 also picked Getting a word in at the right moment, which is the join half of my job that captions alone don't serve.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called a lean, not a call, and the So line refuses to claim it ranks first, so nothing goes past these 7 people.
screens.instead: 7 people, 13 picks (one stopped at one); all 7 put following what's said in their two. Captions answer that, but 3 of 7 also want help getting a word in, so test whether the glasses help them join, not just follow.

screens.why_b1: The card puts 'Holding up' right beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each of my five rungs shows its count and whether it counts for or against, my line sits under 'Missed only a little', and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against out of 7 with the marker at 5, so I take it in at one look.
screens.why_b3: The belief, the act 'following what hearing people said' and the five rungs are the words I saved, and the bar names my rung 'Missed only a little' exactly.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is a generic next step: it does not tell me the gap I have to close is going from 'caught only the gist' to 'missed only a little', or that nobody lost the conversation completely.
screens.why_b5: The card keeps n=7 in view, says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and limits the So line to 'these 7', so it claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7, but mostly in the middle: they caught the gist and lost the detail, and no one lost it outright. The glasses need to move people from 'gist' to 'missed only a little'. The one-sided-loss answer (end seat works) is a hint that single-sided hearing loss is a weaker wedge.

screens.why_b1: The box says Holding up, and 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 sits right beside it, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: It is my Current solution dimension, and the belief line is the one I checked: following what hearing people said still falls short for most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what Tomás's answer means for AirCaps, for example whether people deaf on one side are outside my day-one wedge, and Frequency, the line that actually split, gets no next step at all.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is visible and the held claim fits 6 of 7 against a bar of 5, but the heading 'When a line fails' sits over a line that held, which gives a wrong first read.
screens.why_b6: Tomás, deaf on one side, gets by with an end seat that keeps everyone on his good side; I did not type that, and it marks a group whose seating workaround competes with the glasses.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 (n=7); the one holdout is deaf on one side and gets by with seating, so one-sided loss may sit outside your first buyers. Frequency split 4 to 3 and has no why asked here.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks whether I'm one of the people this study is for, and it's obvious why that comes first.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how I and other deaf people talk about everyone else, so I understand it the first time.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I talk with hearing people at work, in shops and with family, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a screener, and it rightly has no escape option.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'talk with hearing people every week', and nothing about a product or the founder's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is short and is one question, and 'Yes; or No' is easy to hold, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a bit much for a yes-or-no.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or No.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I actually lost track of one of those conversations this past week.
screens.why2: "Lose the thread" is exactly how I'd describe it, when the talk moves on and I'm left nodding without knowing what was said; I could answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether that happened to me at work, at the shop or at dinner this week; it's my own life, not a guess.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and some weeks are quiet one-to-one chats where I truly followed everything, so No is a real answer too.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product reaches me, but the question drops "face-to-face", so I might count a phone or video call, while the next screen asks only about face-to-face talk.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's one short question with "Yes or no" after it, easy to hold and answer, though as a deaf person I'd be reading the captions on screen anyway.
screens.why7: Two fixed answers in order with no escape; the stem asks the thing that goes wrong rather than the weekly routine, so someone who followed every conversation can truly say No and someone who got lost says Yes.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose the thread of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: I just said yes to losing the thread in the last week, so asking how many days that happened is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I'd put it when the talk runs ahead of me, and 'hearing people' is how we say it.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I was at work, at the shop or with family and couldn't keep up, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer without overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits a week where it all blurs.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or a company's plan comes through, only my own week in my own words.
screens.why6: It is one short question, and 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold, though I'd want the words on screen too since I may not hear the voice.
screens.why7: Every option counts days of the 7, starts at 1, ends at 7 and has no 0, the day unit is said once in the window, the event happens on a day, and the one required escape sits apart.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which part of talking with hearing people I'd most want made easier.
screens.why2: Two options say 'their hearing loss' and 'they can see every face' where they mean me, so on first hearing it sounds like the hearing people's hearing loss and I have to read it twice.
screens.why3: Every one of these I actually do or deal with in a conversation, like telling people I'm deaf, jumping in, keeping up, needing a rest from lipreading, and picking where to sit.
screens.why4: The set is real and complete enough and None of these fits, but the pronoun slip makes the first and last options read oddly, and 'Following what hearing people are saying' is so broad that it nearly holds 'Getting a word in' as part of the same thing.
screens.why5: The founder's third-person wording about 'them' leaked into options addressed to me, and 'following' came back as the whole job instead of the moment I lose the thread.
screens.why6: It is one question with five options and one escape, but five options of eight or nine words are a lot to hold by ear, and 'their hearing loss' heard aloud points to the wrong people.
screens.why7: The own item is there, it is not first, there are enough other rows and None of these is at the first ask, but the own row 'Following what hearing people are saying' is half the job said again rather than the part that goes wrong (catching up after I lose the thread), so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Telling people about your hearing loss · Getting a word in at the right moment · Catching up when you lose the thread · Taking a break from listening without leaving · Choosing a seat where you can see every face · None of these

screens.why1: After asking which part of my last conversation I'd most like made easier, asking how well I actually followed it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Following what hearing people said is exactly how I'd talk about it, and each option is a plain amount I'd recognise straight away, though the stem's 'how did following ... go' is a little roundabout.
screens.why3: I know exactly how much I caught in my last conversation, so I can answer from my own week without guessing.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from everything to nothing with no gap or overlap, getting the gist sits sensibly between missing a little and missing most, and 'I can't recall' fits because nobody else could have followed it for me.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's terms reaches me; it only asks how I got on, in words I'd use.
screens.why6: The options are short and easy to hold when heard, but 'How did following what hearing people said go?' is a tangle to catch in one hearing, and the anchor drops 'with hearing people' that the screen before had.
screens.why7: Every rung is on the one measure of how much I followed, the first is today's way working and the last is failing outright, so the belief can be both supported and refuted, and the 'I can't recall' escape is the right one for an act I can't hand off.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of what they said did you follow? Followed everything; missed only a little; caught only the gist; missed most of it; could not follow it at all; or I can't recall.
